episodes.190119: Severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of the 27th over central Oklahoma, along and ahead of the dry line, as a strong upper level low pressure system deepened into the Southern Rockies. Strong instability and strong wind shear over eastern Oklahoma supported organized severe thunderstorms, including supercells. The first round of storms affected portions of far northeastern Oklahoma during the early evening. By late evening, a line of severe thunderstorms moved into eastern Oklahoma from the west, with embedded supercells within the line, as well as a supercell ahead of the line. A strong tornado moved into Okfuskee County with the supercell ahead of the line. Multiple other tornadoes occurred as the storms moved through the area during the early morning hours of the 28th, along with damaging thunderstorm wind gusts. Isolated areas of flash flooding also occurred.||Another round of severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 28th. The strongest storms produced tornadoes, large hail to quarter size, and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.190120: Severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 28th, and moved into northwestern Arkansas during the evening. The thunderstorms produced damaging wind in Benton County, and one of the stronger storms produced a tornado in Carroll County.
episodes.190272: Showers and thunderstorms formed across the area with multiple sea breeze boundaries, energy rounding the base of an upper level ridge and SBCAPE values around 500 to 1000 J/kg. One of these thunderstorms became severe and produced large hail over southeast New York.
episodes.190273: Showers and thunderstorms formed across the area with multiple sea breeze boundaries, energy rounding the base of an upper level ridge and SBCAPE values around 500 to 1000 J/kg. One of these thunderstorms became severe and produced damaging winds over the waters.
episodes.190669: While the main 'piece' of an impactful upper wave lifted into the Northern Plains, a trailing cold front and highly unstable boundary layer fostered the development of a few thunderstorms during the evening of the 28th. While deep-layer wind shear was marginally sufficient (objective analysis showing 30 knots), a few storms became transiently organized and produced a few reports of small hail.
episodes.190703: Thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of April 28th in east Texas along the dryline. As the afternoon and evening progressed, these storms merged together into a mesoscale convective system. The outflow boundary from this MCS drove it southeastward from Texas into Louisiana on the 29th of April. As the leading edge of the storms passed over the local coastal waters, many marine observation platforms measured severe wind gusts.
episodes.190709: A line of thunderstorms entered central and northeast Missouri overnight on April 27th, causing isolated bouts of wind damage and a single tornado before de-intensifying within a few hours of arrival.
episodes.190710: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front as it passed through the area during the early morning of April 29th. The near storm environment was marginal to support widespread severe weather, with only one instance of severe thunderstorm winds reported in Illinois, happening in Madison County.
episodes.190713: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front as it passed through the area during the early morning of April 29th. The near storm environment was unimpressive, and the severe weather threat was forecast to be isolated and marginal. Only one instance of severe thunderstorm winds was reported in Missouri, happening in Washington County.
episodes.190742: Several hours of moderate to heavy rainfall during the night of the 28th into the morning of the 29th caused localized flooding in Tinley Park.
episodes.190842: A line of thunderstorms moved across Southeast Texas causing another round of heavy rain and severe weather. This produced more flooding in areas that had not completely drained from rain earlier in the month.
episodes.190843: A line of thunderstorms swept through Southeast Texas and across Central and South Louisiana. Numerous reports of severe weather and flooding resulted.
episodes.190844: A line of thunderstorms moved along the coast producing high wind gusts.
episodes.190947: Another round of thunderstorms produced additional heavy rainfall and flooding. A severe storm moved across northern Stone County producing a brief EF-0 tornado. Additional wind damage occurred across Cedar and Dade counties.
episodes.191121: By early afternoon, the development of more intense convective activity was recorded over southwest PR. Doppler radar estimated between 2 and 4 inches of rain (locally higher) over the municipalities of the SW of PR, where a Flood Advisory was in effect. Additionally, due to isolated to scattered showers the night before, a landslide was recorded in Canovanas.
episodes.191130: Regenerative thunderstorm development occurred during the afternoon on April 28th across Central Texas along existing outflows from an MCS that decayed earlier in the morning. Surface temperatures continued to warm into the upper 70s to lower 80s within cloud breaks south and east of the large-scale outflow boundary across East Texas and Southwest Arkansas. This led to moderate buoyancy with upper 60s to lower 70s surface dew points. Upscale growth continued along the regenerating MCS as it propagated farther east across the Ark-La-Tex early into the evening. With a favorable deep layer wind profile (0-6km shear near 50 knots), supercells were possible within any emerging thunderstorm clusters. Although shear profiles favored supercells, primary storm mode remained the MCS. Even so, a few tornadoes resulted within embedded circulations, along a few very discrete storm structures that evolved independently of the MCS. Meanwhile, the leading edge of a surging bow echo resulted in widespread damaging winds across Miller and Lafayette Counties with the mature squall line.
episodes.191131: Regenerative thunderstorm development occurred during the afternoon on April 28th across Central Texas along existing outflows from an MCS that decayed earlier in the morning. Surface temperatures continued to warm into the upper 70s to lower 80s within cloud breaks south and east of the large-scale outflow boundary across East Texas into North Louisiana. This led to moderate buoyancy with upper 60s to lower 70s surface dew points. Upscale growth continued along the regenerating MCS as it propagated farther east across the Ark-La-Tex early into the evening. With a favorable deep layer wind profile (0-6km shear near 50 knots), supercells were possible with any emerging thunderstorm clusters. Although shear profiles favored supercells, primary storm mode remained the MCS. Even so, a few tornadoes resulted within embedded circulations, along a few very discrete storm structures that evolved independently of the MCS. Meanwhile, the leading edge of a surging bow echo resulted in widespread damaging winds across Northwest Louisiana with the mature squall line. Given the expanding heavy rain shield and cold pool, an isolated report of flash flooding was also recorded.
episodes.191132: Regenerative thunderstorm development occurred during the afternoon on April 28th across Central Texas along existing outflows from an MCS that decayed earlier in the morning. Surface temperatures continued to warm into the upper 70s to lower 80s within cloud breaks south and east of the large-scale outflow boundary across East Texas. This led to moderate buoyancy with upper 60s to lower 70s surface dew points. Upscale growth continued along the regenerating MCS as it propagated farther east across the Ark-La-Tex early into the evening. With a favorable deep layer wind profile (0-6km shear near 50 knots), supercells were possible within any emerging thunderstorm clusters. Meanwhile, the leading edge of a surging bow echo resulted in widespread damaging winds with a mature squall line along with an isolated report of large hail. Given the expanding heavy rain shield and cold pool, a few reports of flash flooding were also recorded.
episodes.191133: Strong instability and steep lapse rates were present the afternoon and early evening of April 29th across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. A small-scale boundary dropped southward out of far Northeast McCurtain County Oklahoma and Sevier County Arkansas and encountered a very unstable air mass with steep mid-level lapse rates. An isolated supercell thunderstorm developed near the McCurtain County/Sevier County line and moved due south, dropping hail as large as golf ball size along its path. The storm eventually weakened in far Southeast McCurtain County during the late evening hours of April 29th.

An EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 95 mph touched down near the intersection of Dean Road and Cedar Creek Drive and quickly advanced east northeast across residential areas south of Terry Bradshaw Passway. The tornado eventually crossed the above parkway just west of Mansfield Road, then crossed Mansfield Road and ended in the vicinity of Kingston Road. A large majority of the damage was EF-0 level tree damage with just a few pockets of low level EF-1 damage at Southwood High School and just off of Walker Road. At the high school, a weight training facility separated from the main school building lost most of the roof covering, with debris blown hundreds of yards to the north. Otherwise, some structures in the tornado path were damaged by uprooted trees and downed limbs, but fortunately there were no reported injuries or fatalities.

An EF0 tornado with maximum estimated winds near 85 mph touched down near Malone Road and was coincident with a small tornadic debris signature from the KSHV Nexrad Radar. The tornado tracked north northeast for nearly 3 miles across LA Highway 537 and then Still House Road before lifting. Along its path, the tornado uprooted hardwood and softwood trees and broke several large branches before lifting along Still House Road.
A power pole was snapped with a power line pulled away from a home at mile marker 6 on Highway 71 South.
Trees downed on Highway 160 just past County Road 195 east of Doddridge.

An EF1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 100 mph touched down near the intersection of Still House Road and Log Ferry Road, coincident with a small tornadic debris signature from the KSHV Nexrad Radar. The tornado tracked northeast, paralleling Wise Road for a few miles before crossing Clements Road. The tornado produced mainly EF-0 tree damage in the form of uproots and downed limbs. However, there were also quite a few tree trunk snaps as it crossed and lifted along Clements Road just south of the Arkansas state line.
Several trees downed across Highway 71.

An EF-0 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 85 mph touched down along Highway 157 and was coincident with a small tornadic debris signature from the KSHV Nexrad Radar. This tornado tracked north northeast, crossing Chalybeate Springs Road and lifted shortly thereafter. This tornado produced mainly tree damage in the form of uproots and downed limbs along its path.

A short-lived EF1 tornado with maximum estimated winds of 100 mph impacted the Rock Creek Subdivision in Trinity.  The tornado destroyed a mobile home in the subdivision, and two of its occupants sustained injuries.  One of those injured died five days later.  Widespread tree damage and damage to vehicles was also observed along an approximate 500 yard long and 200 yard wide path.

A brief EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 110 mph touched down and tracked east along and just south of County Road 7 in the far southwestern portion of Lafayette County. Despite its short path, the tornado produced higher end EF-1 damage with maximum estimated wind speeds attributed to snapping of power poles and the near destruction of a metal barn housing hay bales. Otherwise, damage was mostly limited to trees in the form of uproots, trunk snaps, and downing of large limbs.
An occupant inside a home on County Road 245 on the south side of Lake Erling was hospitalized with non-life threatening injuries due to a large tree falling onto the home.
Power poles and lines down along CR 246 on the south end of Lake Erling.

A brief EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 90 mph touched down and tracked northeast to the west of Lake Erling, starting along Hood Road and lifting just after crossing Highway 160. The tornado could have begun slightly before Hood Road, but many trees crossing that road limited the survey team's access farther to the southwest. Damage was mostly to trees in the form of uproots, trunk snaps, and downing of large limbs.  ||There were also a multitude of trees downed to the northeast in a widespread area around Lake Erling. Some trees produced structural damage as they fell on residences and the damage was attributed to straight line winds of 60 to 80 mph, not the tornado.

This tornado was observed by storm chasers. It developed south of Heavener and moved east, dissipating southeast of Heavener. The only damage that could be found within its path was snapped tree limbs. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 75 to 80 mph.
